prompt: In the relational schema for the blog example, how is the one-to-many relationship between a post and its comments represented?
choices: A foreign key column on the comments table referencing the post's id
An array of comment ids stored on the posts table
A separate join table linking posts and comments
The comments are embedded directly as a JSON column on posts

prompt: Which MongoDB update operator would you use to change the value of an existing field without touching the rest of the document?
choices: $set
$push
$replace
$field

prompt: Spot the bug: db.products.updateOne({ name: "Widget" }, { price: 9.99 }) is run against a document that also has a category and tags field. What actually happens?
choices: The entire document is replaced with { price: 9.99 }, wiping out category and tags (only _id is preserved)
MongoDB automatically infers you meant $set and only updates price
The update is silently ignored because no operator was given
It throws an error because price is not a valid field name

prompt: A team is building a system where transferring money between two accounts must never leave the books unbalanced, even under concurrent transfers. Which is the better fit, and why?
choices: A relational database, because it provides multi-table ACID transactions with real isolation guarantees
A document database, because embedding both accounts in one document makes the transfer atomic automatically
Either works identically, since both can use $inc / UPDATE for atomic increments
A document database, because schema-on-read makes the transfer faster to develop

prompt: Which scenario is the strongest real fit for a document store over a relational database?
choices: A product catalog where items in different categories have very different, changing sets of attributes
A double-entry accounting ledger
A multi-tenant SaaS billing system with strict referential integrity across invoices and subscriptions
A reporting system that needs ad hoc joins across a dozen normalized tables

prompt: In schema-on-write systems, invalid or mistyped data is typically caught:
choices: At write/insert time, by the database rejecting rows that don't match the declared schema
At read time, by application code that checks each field defensively
Never — schema-on-write systems don't validate data at all
Only during a nightly batch validation job

prompt: A team says: "We're switching our order-processing database from PostgreSQL to MongoDB because MongoDB scales better for big data." Their current Postgres table has 50 million well-indexed rows and no performance complaints. What's the most accurate assessment?
choices: Their reasoning doesn't hold up — a well-indexed Postgres table handles that volume fine, and the choice should be driven by data shape and consistency needs, not raw scale
They're correct — MongoDB always outperforms PostgreSQL once a table exceeds about 10 million rows
They're correct — relational databases cap out around 1 million rows before requiring sharding
It doesn't matter which they pick, since both databases are functionally identical at scale

prompt: Predict the result: db.posts.insertOne({ title: "Hello" }) is run, then immediately db.posts.findOne({ title: "Hello" }). What does the findOne return?
choices: The document { title: "Hello", _id: <auto-generated ObjectId> }
null, because findOne requires an explicit _id filter
The document without any _id field, since none was provided on insert
